FIRST WARN FORECAST
Tuesday, September 1, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

HEAT ADVISORY THROUGH FRIDAY EVENING

Welcome to the first day of meteorological fall. September 1 marks the beginning of meteorological fall, but our weather will feel anything but fall-like this week.

A Heat Advisory remains in effect for the entire First Warn Weather coverage area through Friday evening as a prolonged period of unseasonably hot weather continues across central Missouri, the St. Louis metropolitan area, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois.

Afternoon temperatures will generally climb into the middle and upper 90s through the end of the work week, with a few locations potentially approaching 100 degrees. Combined with humidity, heat index values will reach approximately 98 to 105 degrees during the afternoon hours.

The duration of this heat remains one of the primary concerns. We are looking at several consecutive days of temperatures well above normal for early September, so heat precautions will remain important throughout the week.

HOT AND DRY TUESDAY

A strong upper-level ridge of high pressure is centered over southern Missouri this morning. This large area of high pressure is responsible for the persistent hot and dry conditions across the Mid-Mississippi Valley.

At the surface, winds remain from the south and southwest, continuing to transport very warm air into the region. Temperatures several thousand feet above the surface remain exceptionally warm, supporting another afternoon of temperatures well into the 90s.

Highs Tuesday will generally reach the middle to upper 90s across central Missouri, the St. Louis area, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois. A few of the warmer locations could approach 100 degrees.

Humidity levels may be somewhat lower than some computer guidance suggests. Recent dry weather, the later point in the growing season, and southwest winds descending from the Ozark Plateau should help keep dewpoints from becoming excessively high.

However, the combination of upper 90s and moderate humidity will still produce heat index values between approximately 98 and 105 degrees.

WEDNESDAY BRINGS LITTLE CHANGE

There will be very little change in our weather Wednesday.

The center of the upper-level high will slowly shift eastward, but south-to-southwest flow will remain firmly established across Missouri and Illinois.

Expect another mostly sunny, dry, and very hot day with afternoon temperatures in the middle to upper 90s. Some locations may once again approach the 100-degree mark.

Heat index values will again reach approximately 98 to 105 degrees during the afternoon.

The strong ridge of high pressure will also continue to suppress meaningful shower and thunderstorm development, so widespread rainfall is not expected.

HEAT CONTINUES THURSDAY AND FRIDAY

The upper-level ridge will begin shifting back toward the west later this week, but that process will not happen quickly enough to provide immediate relief.

Thursday and Friday will remain unseasonably hot.

High temperatures will continue well into the 90s across the region, while afternoon heat index values should remain near or above 100 degrees in many locations.

The Heat Advisory currently remains in effect through Friday evening.

With several consecutive days of significant heat expected, it is important not to focus exclusively on whether temperatures reach 100 degrees. The cumulative effects of prolonged heat can become increasingly dangerous, particularly for people who work outdoors, older adults, young children, those without reliable air conditioning, and anyone particularly sensitive to heat.

WATCHING THE WEEKEND FOR SOME RELIEF

There are indications that the weather pattern may finally begin changing this weekend, although the timing remains uncertain.

Saturday could still be quite hot. Current guidance continues to support afternoon temperatures well into the 90s, with heat index values potentially exceeding 100 degrees again.

Because of this, an extension of the Heat Advisory into Saturday may eventually become necessary. That decision will depend on temperature and humidity trends over the next several days.

A weak cold front is expected to approach from the east or northeast during the weekend. The timing of that boundary will determine how quickly temperatures begin to moderate.

A faster arrival would provide some relief Saturday. A slower progression would allow the significant heat to continue through much of Saturday before somewhat cooler air arrives Sunday.

At this point, Saturday appears likely to remain the hotter of the two weekend days.

LIMITED RAINFALL WITH THE FRONT

While the approaching front may eventually provide some temperature relief, it does not currently appear likely to produce widespread rainfall.

The strong upper-level ridge will continue to suppress thunderstorm development across much of the region.

Only about 25 percent of our longer-range ensemble guidance produces measurable precipitation between Saturday and Labor Day.

There could certainly be an isolated shower or thunderstorm near the front, but widespread beneficial rainfall does not appear likely at this time.

Temperatures behind the front should moderate somewhat Sunday into early next week, although highs may still remain in the 90s.

HEAT SAFETY REMAINS IMPORTANT

With a Heat Advisory continuing through Friday evening, heat safety should remain a priority throughout the week.

Stay hydrated and take frequent breaks if you are spending extended periods outdoors. Whenever possible, schedule strenuous outdoor activities during the morning or evening rather than during the hottest portion of the afternoon.

Check on elderly relatives, friends, and neighbors, particularly those without reliable air conditioning.

Pets should have constant access to fresh water and shade. Pavement temperatures can also become dangerously hot during the afternoon.

Never leave children or animals inside a parked vehicle, even for a short period of time.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Meteorological fall officially begins today, but summer heat will remain firmly in control of our weather.

A Heat Advisory is in effect for the entire First Warn Weather coverage area through Friday evening.

High temperatures Tuesday through Friday will generally reach the middle to upper 90s, with a few locations potentially approaching 100 degrees. Afternoon heat index values will range from approximately 98 to 105 degrees.

Saturday may remain hot enough that an extension of the Heat Advisory becomes necessary.

A weak cold front could finally provide some relief later in the weekend, with Sunday currently expected to be somewhat cooler. However, even behind the front, temperatures may remain in the 90s into early next week.

The calendar may say meteorological fall, but the atmosphere remains firmly in a summertime pattern.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

Central Illinois
Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

🟤 Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5)

Central Missouri
Eastern Missouri
St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

🟡 Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5)

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

🟢 Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5)

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
